LETTER:
To the Road Authority

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). In that time there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.1 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.

There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A van at 18.0 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.
A car at 47.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s in the close pass category. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

During 7.7 minutes (462.0 s) of video at Market Street crossing, Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 29 moving vehicles. 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 15.2-72.3% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The recording contained 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 2 times the person was first and 3 times the vehicle was first.

The worst events were: A serious near-miss with PET of 0.8 s involving a car at 32.7 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had PET of 0.8 s involving a motorcycle at 27.9 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss had PET of 0.6 s involving a motorcycle at 18.0 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at 18.0 km/h. A close pass had PET of 1.9 s involving a bus at 58.6 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. A further close pass had PET of 2.2 s involving a car at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front.

Engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this one is 7.7. 48.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap including 1 of 12 s or more and longest 84.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We offer to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

The other close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.6 km/h with 2.1 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% death risk.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.6 minutes with 7 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles. We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians. We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). In that time there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.1 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 55.2 km/h.

There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A van at 18.0 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.
A car at 47.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s in the close pass category. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Cedar Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch tracking using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry over 31.5 minutes recorded 29 crossings and 28 vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 48.0 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.1 s the vehicle was going at 44.4 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.5 s it was going at 42.2 km/h.

In that time 5 of 29 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 1 of 29 (1 in 29) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.8-35.8% and 0.1-17.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst events were post-encroachment time measured as serious below 1.5 s and close pass 1.5-3.0 s. A serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s as a car passed at 42.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 4.3%.
A close pass had a gap of 1.5 s as a car passed at 44.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s as a van passed at 35.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
A close pass had a gap of 2.5 s as a motorcycle passed at 38.5 km/h.
A close pass had a gap of 2.8 s as a car passed at 33.6 km/h.
All death-risk figures are Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts at 20 km/h limit the impact would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% risk in these cases.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 55 pedestrians and 53 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.5 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 55.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 10.0 s, where the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce approach speeds and give priority to pupils crossing. We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write to request a raised zebra crossing at the Hill View Road crossing following video measurements made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 27.7 minutes (1662.0 s) we counted 28 crossings and 18 vehicles.

3 of 28 crossings (1 in 9.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 28 (1 in 14) within 1.5 s.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 2.3-28.2% and 0.9-23.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s, with the person first in 3 cases.

The 85th percentile speed was 60.2 km/h.

1 serious near-miss involved a van at 57.7 km/h with 0.8 s between the person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 15.3%, compared with 0.0 km/h and 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious near-miss involved a car at 23.0 km/h with 0.1 s between the person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 0.8%, compared with 20.0 km/h and 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

1 close pass involved a van at 15.2 km/h with 2.8 s between the person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 0.0%, compared with 0.0 km/h and 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 61 pedestrians and 39 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 27.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour.

80.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.2 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority to people crossing.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Hill View Road crossing. A 6.9 minute video (414.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. 3 of 7 crossings (1 in 2.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person; 0 of 7 within 1.5 s. By definition there were 0 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

One close pass involved a bus at 43.3 km/h with 1.6 s between road users, with an adult death risk of 3.8% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). This change is certain to save lives at this crossing. A second close pass involved a bus at 56.8 km/h with 2.4 s between road users, with an adult death risk of 1.0% if hit. A third close pass involved a bus at 12.4 km/h with 1.9 s between road users.

The 85th percentile speed was 60.4 km/h. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is only 6.9 minutes, so we counted 7 crossings and 4 vehicles without calculating rates. 76.2% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 6 gaps with longest 7.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing point. We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane crossing.

Measurements from Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) over 17.7 minutes (1062.0 s) recorded 13 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.

There were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 4, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst cases were:
The 1st serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 47.5 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 6.8 % (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 2nd serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.7 km/h with 0.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 4.9 %, with 20.0 km/h impact and 0.6 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 3rd serious near-miss involved a car at 39.8 km/h with 1.1 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 3.5 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 4th serious near-miss involved a car at 33.1 km/h with 1.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 1.9 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 44 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count. 51.9 % of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 42.3 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians. We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully
The Principal

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street. From a Crossing Watch analysis of 32.8 minutes of video we recorded 25 crossings and 20 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.2 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.

There was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a bus at 25.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which at a 20 km/h limit would be an impact of 20.0 km/h with 0.6% risk.

A close pass had a gap of 1.5 s with a bus at 24.8 km/h and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.9%, which at a 20 km/h limit would be an impact of 6.3 km/h with 0.2% risk.

Another close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a car at 53.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.0%, which at a 20 km/h limit would be an impact of 0.0 km/h with 0.0% risk.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 46 pedestrians and 37 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.8 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. Also 78.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 9 gaps with 3 of them 12 s or more and longest 20.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch review of 30.3 minutes (1818.0 s) of video at North Avenue crossing recorded 17 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 40.8 km/h. Drivers at this location are regularly exceeding the speed limit. In that period 2 of 17 crossings (1 in 8.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, of which 1 of 17 (1 in 17) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.5-36.4% and 0.1-28.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s between the person and a bus travelling at 36.8 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates that an adult hit by a car front at that speed has a 2.7% death risk, compared with 0.2% death risk at an impact of 7.5 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A second close pass had a gap of 2.9 s from a bus travelling at 28.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 30.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. In the recording, 47.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 8 gaps including 6 of 12 s or more with longest 13.6 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We hold the video and tracking data and would be pleased to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school beside Orchard Lane crossing. From video of the crossing we measured 10 crossings and 39 vehicles in 17.2 minutes (1032.0 s), with an 85th percentile speed of 60.5 km/h.

6 of 10 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 10 (1 in 3.3) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 26.2-87.8% and 6.7-65.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition serious is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. Person first was 4, vehicle first was 2 and both at once was 0.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 53.4 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. Another serious near-miss involved a van at 44.1 km/h with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 14.6 km/h with 0.1 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

One close pass involved a bus at 36.1 km/h with 1.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 31.1 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

For adults hit by a car front, the modelled death risks for those events would be 11.0% for the motorcycle case, 5.1% for the van case, 0.4% for the car case, 1.6% for the bus case and 0.7% for the auto-rickshaw case (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 35 pedestrians and 136 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice, 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 51.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest 38.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to enforce lower speeds at the conflict point and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and measurement log for your review and to discuss further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

At the Park Avenue crossing, Crossing Watch video of 44.8 minutes recorded 15 crossings and 10 vehicles with 85th percentile speed of 56.6 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

By the Crossing Watch definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

In that period there were 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes, with 0 person first, 3 vehicle first and 0 both at once.

The most serious event was 1.3 s apart involving a van at 58.0 km/h with 15.7% adult death risk if hit.

A close pass was 2.4 s apart involving a motorcycle at 55.0 km/h with 0.8% adult death risk if hit.

A further close pass was 2.8 s apart involving a car at 59.3 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk if hit.

Death risks are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

On engineering, PV2 = 0.0 x 10^8 from 20 pedestrians and 13 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.8 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.

Also 79.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.4 s, noting edge effects cut short by the video.

I request 1 raised zebra crossing at the Park Avenue crossing to slow traffic and protect school children.

I offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on River Lane outside our school. We monitored the crossing by video for 24.7 minutes (1482.0 s) and counted 14 pedestrian crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.9 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart, with 2 cases where the vehicle arrived first, 0 where the person arrived first and 0 where both arrived at once.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and involved a car travelling at 41.4 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 4.0%, compared with 0.2% if impact were at 5.8 km/h under a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a bus travelling at 30.5 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact were at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

For context, engineering estimates scale to 34 pedestrians and 39 vehicles an hour to give PV² = 0.0 x 10^8, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x due to broken tracks, scaled from 24.7 minutes of video.
84.9% of the observed time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 35.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce approach speeds and give priority to those crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning the crossing on River Lane outside our school. We monitored the crossing by video for 24.7 minutes (1482.0 s) and counted 14 pedestrian crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact were at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

During 7.7 minutes (462.0 s) of video at Market Street crossing, Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 29 moving vehicles. 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. The recording contained 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 2 times the person was first and 3 times the vehicle was first.

The worst events were: A serious near-miss with PET of 0.8 s involving a car at 32.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had PET of 0.8 s involving a motorcycle at 27.9 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss had PET of 0.6 s involving a motorcycle at 18.0 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at 18.0 km/h. A close pass had PET of 1.9 s involving a bus at 58.6 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. A further close pass had PET of 2.2 s involving a car at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front.

Engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this one is 7.7. 48.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap including 1 of 12 s or more and longest 84.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We offer to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write on behalf of the school regarding safety at Lantern Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis of video covering 7.0 minutes recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles. A third serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 15.2 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4%.
A close pass involved a car at 50.0 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s with an adult death risk if hit of 1.7%.
A close pass involved a van at 24.9 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s with an adult death risk if hit of 0.0%.

Engineering context notes PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.0 minutes, so counts are limited. In that period 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps including 11 of 12 s or more and longest 89.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

During 34.5 minutes (2070.0 s) at School Lane crossing we recorded 14 crossings and 36 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.6 km/h. Traffic has gotten much worse at this crossing compared to last year.

6 of 14 crossings (1 in 2.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s. 3 of 14 (1 in 4.7) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 17.7-71.1% and 4.7-50.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe near-miss was PET 0.0 s. The vehicle was an auto-rickshaw at 46.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At 20.0 km/h the death risk would be 0.6%.

A 2nd serious near-miss was PET 0.4 s. The vehicle was a car at 42.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.4%. At 20.0 km/h the death risk would be 0.6%.

A 3rd serious near-miss was PET 1.3 s. The vehicle was a car at 40.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6%. At 20.0 km/h the death risk would be 0.0%.

There were also 3 close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. One close pass was PET 1.9 s. The vehicle was a motorcycle at 50.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.2%.

Another close pass was PET 1.5 s. The vehicle was a car at 37.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.8%.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 24 pedestrians and 63 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 34.5 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. 92.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on School Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school at School Lane crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 11.7 minutes (702.0 s) with 10 pedestrian crossings and 24 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.2 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 
93.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and longest 89.0 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

There was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 
The serious near-miss had PET of 0.0 s and involved a car at 43.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 4.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
The first close pass had PET of 1.6 s and involved a motorcycle at 47.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 5.3%.
The second close pass had PET of 2.7 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 21.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 0.0%.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for pupils.

We can share the video and measurement files on request and welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Hill View Road crossing. A video recording lasting 42.7 minutes (2562.0 s) measured 39 crossings and 10 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.1 km/h. During 42.7 minutes the count was 39 crossings and 10 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 60.1 km/h.

The recording found 2 of 39 crossings (1 in 20) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 39 (1 in 39) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.6-17.3% and 0.1-13.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 54.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the source Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts gives an 11.7% death risk.

A second close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a motorcycle travelling at 16.5 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 42.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in the drone test. Also, 86.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap and a longest gap of 11.3 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a van at 24.9 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.4%).
Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (18 pedestrians and 15 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 27.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We have the video and data on file and are happy to share them to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school I am requesting a safety improvement at the Station Road crossing.

A video survey of 28.1 minutes (1686.0 s) recorded 27 crossings and 26 vehicles at this location. The 85th percentile speed was 59.8 km/h. In total 4 of 27 crossings (1 in 6.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 27 (1 in 9) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 4.2-33.7% and 2.4-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 4 closest events were:
One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.5 km/h passing the same spot 0.9 s apart, with an adult death risk of 14.0% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 33.8 km/h passing 0.7 s apart, with an adult death risk of 2.1% if hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 13.6 km/h passing 0.8 s apart, with an adult death risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.
A close pass involved a van at 31.3 km/h passing 2.0 s apart, with an adult death risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 28.1 minutes to 58 pedestrians and 56 vehicles an hour, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 97.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 2 such gaps and a longest gap of 7.1 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this site to reduce speeds and provide a formal priority for people crossing. A child struck at 56.5 km/h at this crossing would have had a 38% probability of death.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing as the school using Market Street crossing. We commissioned video monitoring of the crossing.

Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 16.6 minutes (996.0 s). In that time 26 crossings and 41 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 53.2 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the near-misses, 3 were person-first, 2 were vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 54.0 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 11.5% per Rosen & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 43.9 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 5.0% per the same source.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 28.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% per the same source.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 26.6 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.1% per the same source.
One close pass involved a van at 36.8 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% per the same source.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 148 vehicles an hour scaled from 16.6 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. Also, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 7 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.6 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write to request a safety improvement at the Quarry Road crossing.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 49.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 8.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 37.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 2.9%. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 19.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 0.6%. One close pass involved a car at 47.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 2.5%. Another close pass involved a car at 31.7 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 0.0%.

We therefore request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are happy to share the full 7.5 minute video and the detailed measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements made by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) at the Park Avenue crossing. In 38.5 minutes of video, equivalent to 2310.0 s, 38 people crossed and 7 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 53.2 km/h. Speeds at this crossing have been getting worse every month this year.

The video recorded 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded for 4 interactions, vehicle first for 0, and both at once for 0.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 51.2 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 49.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.9%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a bus at 21.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One close pass had a gap of 1.5 s with a car at 52.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.9%.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8, from 59 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also, 64.5% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 27.9 s, noting that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We are willing to share the original video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

We write about safety at the River Lane crossing. In 19.2 minutes at River Lane crossing, 15 crossings and 24 vehicles were observed. Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 19.2 minutes (1152.0 s) with 15 crossings and 24 vehicles.

During that period 5 of 15 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 15 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-61.6% and 4.3-48.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.5 km/h.

The worst serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 49.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 22.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a van at 14.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van at 40.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a car at 47.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.4%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (47 pedestrians and 75 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 19.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 64.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 4 of 12 s or more and the longest 27.1 s (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school I am requesting a safety improvement at the Station Road crossing.

A video survey of 28.1 minutes (1686.0 s) recorded 27 crossings and 26 vehicles at this location. The 85th percentile speed was 59.8 km/h. In total 4 of 27 crossings (1 in 6.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 27 (1 in 9) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 4.2-33.7% and 2.4-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 4 closest events were:
One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.5 km/h passing the same spot 0.9 s apart, with an adult death risk of 14.0% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 33.8 km/h passing 0.7 s apart, with an adult death risk of 2.1% if hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 13.6 km/h passing 0.8 s apart, with an adult death risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.
A close pass involved a van at 31.3 km/h passing 2.0 s apart, with an adult death risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 28.1 minutes to 58 pedestrians and 56 vehicles an hour, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 97.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 2 such gaps and a longest gap of 7.1 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this site to reduce speeds and provide a formal priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at North Avenue crossing

We asked for video measurements at the North Avenue crossing outside our school. In 34.8 minutes (2088.0 s) of video, 25 crossings and 12 vehicles were observed, with an 85th percentile speed of 61.5 km/h.

Of the 25 crossings, 3 of 25 crossings (1 in 8.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 25 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 2.5-31.2% and 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Most of the close encounters involved young schoolchildren crossing without an adult.

The most severe was a serious near-miss with 0.7 s between person and vehicle, the car travelling at 57.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% death risk.

A 2nd serious near-miss had 0.0 s between person and vehicle, the car travelling at 12.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had 2.4 s between person and vehicle, the motorcycle travelling at 36.7 km/h. For an adult hit the death risk is 0.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, scaled from this 34.8 minutes, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 43 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour. A formal check counts the full peak hour, and pedestrians are people who walked 2 m or more on the marked carriageway, or anywhere in view if none is marked, and broken tracks can count 1 person twice: 1.3x the true count in the drone test.

Also, 65.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.8 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Bridge Street crossing

We write as the school beside Bridge Street crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 40.5 minutes of video (2430.0 s) recorded 14 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.8 km/h.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 24.4 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s. At that speed an adult hit by a car front would face a 0.9% death risk, compared with 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 19.0 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s. At that speed an adult hit by a car front would face a 0.6% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.0 km/h.

There was also a close pass with a van at 47.2 km/h with a gap of 2.6 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 21 pedestrians and 41 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 40.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in tests. Also, 43.2% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 32.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing outside our school on Brook Street.

In 6.5 minutes of video (390.0 s) we counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 2 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 37.0 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events.

PV² and hourly rate assessment requires at least 15 minutes of video, so this 6.5 minute sample is too short for that calculation.

40.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps including 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 83.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious near-miss involved a car travelling at 38.4 km/h.

The time gap for that event was 0.7 s.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 3.1%, compared with 0.6% if impact were at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For these reasons we request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

We measured activity at Garden Road crossing from video of 34.8 minutes, using SAM tracking and post-encroachment time. In that period there were 25 crossings and 13 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.9 km/h. We recorded 6 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, with 3 where the person was first and 3 where the vehicle was first.

The worst cases were: One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.2 s with a car at 58.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 16.0% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 31.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a bus at 27.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.2% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a van at 25.7 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.0% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car at 22.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit by a car front. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 43 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 34.8 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. Also, 51.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 gaps and longest gap 8.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone markings and signs at this location. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning Orchard Lane crossing. In 28.8 minutes (1728.0 s) of video we recorded 24 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 38.8 km/h. Of the 24 crossings, 4 of 24 (1 in 6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s and 3 of 24 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s.

The recording showed 3 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 32.1 km/h with a PET of 0.7 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 31.6 km/h with a PET of 0.9 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.7%.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.7 km/h with a PET of 1.4 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6%.

The close pass involved a car at 17.0 km/h with a PET of 1.8 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.2%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 28.8 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 45.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps and longest 76.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower vehicle speeds and protect people crossing. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch review of 30.3 minutes (1818.0 s) of video at North Avenue crossing recorded 17 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 40.8 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings. In that period 2 of 17 crossings (1 in 8.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, of which 1 of 17 (1 in 17) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.5-36.4% and 0.1-28.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s between the person and a bus travelling at 36.8 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates that an adult hit by a car front at that speed has a 2.7% death risk, compared with 0.2% death risk at an impact of 7.5 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A second close pass had a gap of 2.9 s from a bus travelling at 28.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 30.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. In the recording, 47.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 8 gaps including 6 of 12 s or more with longest 13.6 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We hold the video and tracking data and would be pleased to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The other serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a car travelling at 27.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 27.1 km/h the death risk is 1.1%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing regarding the safety of the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time were made over 21.9 minutes, equal to 1314.0 s, during which 24 crossings and 39 vehicles were recorded. In 1314.0 s there were 24 crossings and 39 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. In that period there were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded in 4 cases and vehicle first in 1 case, with 0 cases of both at once.

The worst serious near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious near-miss a bus travelling at 49.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit by the front of a car at that speed the death risk would be 8.0% per Rosen and Sander 2009 for adults 15+ and at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 2nd serious near-miss a car travelling at 28.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.3% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 3rd serious near-miss a bus travelling at 26.0 km/h was 0.2 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.0% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. 2 further close passes had PET of 2.0 s and 2.9 s with vehicle speeds of 12.9 km/h and 33.6 km/h.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 66 pedestrians and 107 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 21.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice with 1.3x inflation in a drone test. 85.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps and 8 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 17.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6 notes that 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone and signs at Lantern Road crossing.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review. Please let us know how you wish to receive them.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal
Approved by The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

We are writing about the safety of the Orchard Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch measured the crossing with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry for 35.4 minutes (2124.0 s). In that time there were 9 crossings and 10 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 46.4 km/h.

Of the 9 crossings, 2 of 9 crossings (1 in 4.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.8-60.0% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. The most serious involved a bus at 39.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. At 39.2 km/h the death risk if an adult is hit by a car front is 3.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

The other serious near-miss involved a car at 32.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. At 32.0 km/h the death risk if an adult is hit by a car front is 1.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (15 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour), scaled from 35.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. 91.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (4 gaps, longest 10.7 s; the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority. We have the video and measurement data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

In that short period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to record the Garden Road crossing for 3.2 minutes (192.0 s). In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 37.0 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

The definition used was serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes. In 4 cases the person was first to the conflict point, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both arrived at once.

The worst near-miss was a serious conflict with a motorcycle at 38.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 3.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would fall to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was with an auto-rickshaw at 19.3 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Among the close passes, one involved an auto-rickshaw at 14.1 km/h with a gap of 1.5 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4%. Another involved a bus at 16.7 km/h with a gap of 1.6 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4%.

For context, 71.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (6 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 71.0 s). The main caveat is that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 3.2 minutes, and the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians clear priority.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the School Lane crossing safer

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at School Lane crossing. We commissioned a video review of the crossing from Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).

What was measured: the video covered 9.2 minutes (552.0 s). In that period we counted 4 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.0 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

Engineering context with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 9.2. 46.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.2 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). That 9.2 minute period included 1 gap of at least 6 s and 1 gap of at least 12 s, the longest of which was 47.2 s.

Worst near-misses:
One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. The vehicle speed was 58.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 11.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.3%.
One serious near-miss involved a bus with a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s. The vehicle speed was 56.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

Requested fix: we ask you to install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We have the video and data on file and are happy to share them to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
