LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write following a 15.4 minutes (924.0 s) video recording at Quarry Road crossing. In that period we counted 36 crossings and 2 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 20.8 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

1 of 36 crossings (1 in 36) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 1 of 36 (1 in 36) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.1-14.5% and 0.1-14.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We recorded 1 serious near-miss defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 0 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. The worst case was a serious near-miss with PET of 1.3 s involving a car. The car was travelling at 13.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 13.5 km/h the death risk is 0.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 140 pedestrians and 8 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 15.4 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x. 71.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 4 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 30.2 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at School Lane crossing

We write regarding pedestrian safety outside our school at School Lane crossing. During 37.0 minutes, cameras logged 40 crossings and 20 vehicles. Crossing Watch video measurements over 37.0 minutes (2220.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 20 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 45.7 km/h.

A 2nd close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.5 km/h with a gap of 2.7 s to a person.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review. Please advise on next steps for assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

We are writing about the safety of the Orchard Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch measured the crossing with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry for 35.4 minutes (2124.0 s). In that time there were 9 crossings and 10 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 46.4 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school.

Of the 9 crossings, 2 of 9 crossings (1 in 4.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.8-60.0% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. The most serious involved a bus at 39.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. At 39.2 km/h the death risk if an adult is hit by a car front is 3.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the Quarry Road crossing.

We had 7.5 minutes of video analysed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that period of 450.0 s, 10 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h.

There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of 5 interactions, 0 had the person first, 5 had the vehicle first and 0 had both at once.

Engineering note: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.5 minutes. Counted: 10 pedestrian crossings, 25 moving vehicles. 83.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 17.8 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 49.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 8.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 37.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 2.9%. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 19.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 0.6%. One close pass involved a car at 47.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 2.5%. Another close pass involved a car at 31.7 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s and an estimated adult death risk if hit of 0.0%.

We therefore request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location. A child struck here would face an extremely high likelihood of death.

We are happy to share the full 7.5 minute video and the detailed measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 19.7 minutes. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Park Avenue crossing. A video review using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time covered 9.9 minutes (594.0 s) and recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.8 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.

Across the review there were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart. In 1 case the person was first, in 3 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.0 s with a car travelling at 50.4 km/h; if an adult were hit by the car front at that speed the estimated death risk would be 8.6% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
Another serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.1 s with a car travelling at 45.6 km/h; the estimated adult death risk at that speed would be 5.7%.
A third serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 14.8 km/h; the estimated adult death risk would be 0.4%.
A close pass had a time gap of 2.0 s with a car travelling at 39.7 km/h; the estimated adult death risk would be 0.9%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 9.9 minutes with 5 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles, so results should be treated with caution. 65.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 such gaps including 10 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school by Garden Road crossing, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Our Crossing Watch video covered 27.4 minutes (1644.0 s) and recorded 8 crossings and 7 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.7 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. In that period we recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, with 3 person-first, 2 vehicle-first and 1 both at once.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 55.9 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 13.4%).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 48.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 7.1%).
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a car at 45.2 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 5.6%).
A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 20.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.6%).
One close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a van at 24.9 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.4%).
Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (18 pedestrians and 15 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 27.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour).
79.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.6 s (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst events were as follows.
The most severe serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a motorcycle at 51.2 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% and would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a motorcycle at 24.7 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.9% and would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 46.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 6.2% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 40 pedestrians and 24 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 40.2 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count by 1.3x in drone tests.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing on behalf of our school about safety at the Canal Road crossing. A 6.4 minute video recording, duration 384.0 s, at the crossing measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 44 moving vehicles.

85th percentile speed was 60.5 km/h. Analysis used SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

In that period, 6 of 6 crossings, 1 in 1, had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s. 5 of 6, 1 in 1.2, were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1 to 100.0% and 35.9 to 99.6% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 2.2 to 13.1 and 1.6 to 11.7 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

2 crossings had the person first and 4 had the vehicle first, with 0 both at once. 1 was a close pass and 5 were serious near-misses.

Details of the serious near-misses, with adult death risk if hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus, car fronts:

The first involved a bus at 54.4 km/h with a time gap of 0.5 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 11.8%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The second involved a van at 51.9 km/h with a time gap of 0.1 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 9.7%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The third involved a van at 31.6 km/h with a time gap of 1.0 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 1.7%, compared to impact at 17.9 km/h and 0.5% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The fourth involved a motorcycle at 26.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 1.1%, compared to impact at 6.3 km/h and 0.2% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The fifth involved a motorcycle at 20.5 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 0.6%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.4, with 6 crossings and 44 vehicles counted. 60.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 17.6 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch data for your review. Thank you for your consideration.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

I write as head of the school at Mill Street crossing to request safety improvements.

We arranged a video review of the crossing covering 22.6 minutes (1356.0 s). In that time 14 crossings and 21 vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 47.1 km/h. There were 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, with the longest gap at 73.7 s. The count found 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 1 case the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first, with 0 cases of both at once. Three of the four dangerous encounters involved schoolchildren on their way to class.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.0 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s; the estimated adult death risk if hit is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 15.6 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s. Another close pass involved a motorcycle at 14.1 km/h with a gap of 2.7 s.

Engineering review notes PV² as 0.0 x 10^8, based on 37 pedestrians and 56 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. It also notes that 91.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide a safer crossing for pupils.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

As Principal of the school by the Lake View Road crossing I write to request safety improvements based on video measurements.

We observed the crossing for 18.8 minutes (1128.0 s) and recorded 5 crossings and 7 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.1 km/h. In 1128.0 s there were 5 crossings and 7 vehicles, including 1 serious near-miss with a PET of 0.8 s at 21.3 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, with 2 cases where the person went first.

The most serious event was a car passing 0.8 s after a pedestrian at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 0.7% and at an impact of 20.0 km/h it would be 0.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The second event was a car passing 1.8 s after a pedestrian at 39.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 1.6% and at an impact of 0.0 km/h it would be 0.0%.

For context the video scales to PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 16 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour, though a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

About 66.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 9 gaps of which 5 were 12 s or more with a longest gap of 72.5 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.0 s the vehicle was going at 44.4 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.5 s it was going at 58.9 km/h.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A bus at 58.9 km/h was 1.0 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Canal Road crossing outside our school. From video we measured 4 pedestrian crossings and 15 vehicles in 3.1 minutes (186.0 s), with an 85th percentile speed of 48.1 km/h. The 3.1 minute recording contained 4 crossings and 15 vehicles and lasted 186.0 s.

The most serious encounter involved an auto-rickshaw at 47.7 km/h passing 0.4 s after the person at the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.8% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h) per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
The other close pass involved a bus at 20.3 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.1% (0.0% at 20.0 km/h).

Gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed covered 42.3% of the time, with 4 such gaps and a longest gap of 7.2 s. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.1 minutes with 4 crossings and 15 vehicles, and the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h signs at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. By these figures the crossing already qualifies for a signal-controlled crossing.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing regarding the safety of the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time were made over 21.9 minutes, equal to 1314.0 s, during which 24 crossings and 39 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. Most drivers were exceeding the posted speed limit by a wide margin. In that period there were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded in 4 cases and vehicle first in 1 case, with 0 cases of both at once.

The worst serious near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious near-miss a bus travelling at 49.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit by the front of a car at that speed the death risk would be 8.0% per Rosen and Sander 2009 for adults 15+ and at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 2nd serious near-miss a car travelling at 28.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.3% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 3rd serious near-miss a bus travelling at 26.0 km/h was 0.2 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.0% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. 2 further close passes had PET of 2.0 s and 2.9 s with vehicle speeds of 12.9 km/h and 33.6 km/h.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 66 pedestrians and 107 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 21.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice with 1.3x inflation in a drone test. 85.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps and 8 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 17.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6 notes that 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone and signs at Lantern Road crossing.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review. Please let us know how you wish to receive them.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Station Road outside our school, where we made video measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

During 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) we observed 12 pedestrian crossings and 20 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.
3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s.
If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 5.5-57.2% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For context on gaps, 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.7 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.
PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.1, with 12 crossings and 20 vehicles counted.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.
We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and involved a car at 29.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.3 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s and involved a van at 32.1 km/h.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the video and measurements available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.4 s the vehicle was going at 40.3 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.9 s it was going at 44.5 km/h. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Park Avenue crossing outside our school. In a video recording lasting 11.6 minutes (696.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 18 moving vehicles.

In that period, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 0 of 6 had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.0-45.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-3.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s) and 0 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s). Of the close passes, 2 were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first. The 85th percentile speed was 26.5 km/h. Most parents told us they feel unsafe letting their children use this crossing alone.

The worst close pass was 2.1 s apart with the car at 23.8 km/h. A second close pass was 2.6 s apart with the car at 26.8 km/h. A third close pass was 2.9 s apart with the car at 19.6 km/h.

Engineering context from the same recording: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.6 minutes, so no rate can be calculated. 50.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write to request consideration of a raised zebra crossing at North Avenue crossing outside our school.

We commissioned video analysis of 16.3 minutes (978.0 s) at this location. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.9-23.5% and 0.1-18.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The video covering 978.0 s counted 28 crossings and 13 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.7 km/h and 12 gaps of at least 6 s including 4 gaps of at least 12 s up to 26.7 s.

There were 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Vehicle first occurred in 2 cases.

The most serious event involved a bus passing 1.1 s after the person at 43.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second event involved a van passing 2.8 s after the person at 23.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.0% on the same source.

We request that you assess and install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request and welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Lantern Road crossing outside our school.

A 9.1 minute (546.0 s) video recorded by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured 3 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. In the serious case the post-encroachment time was 0.3 s between the pedestrian and a bus travelling at 19.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 19.7 km/h the death risk is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

In the close pass case the post-encroachment time was 1.8 s between the pedestrian and a bus travelling at 21.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

We request the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table to provide a protected priority crossing and to reduce vehicle speeds at the conflict point.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety at the Park Avenue crossing outside our school.

A 3.7 minute video (222.0 s) recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 43 moving vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 59.1 mph. There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 6 close interactions, 3 were person first and 3 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
One serious near-miss involved a bus at 55.6 km/h with 1.3 s between road users and an adult death risk if hit of 13.1%.
One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 47.1 km/h with 0.8 s between road users and an adult death risk if hit of 6.5%.
One serious near-miss involved a car at 41.5 km/h with 1.4 s between road users and an adult death risk if hit of 4.1%.
One serious near-miss involved a car at 34.4 km/h with 1.3 s between road users and an adult death risk if hit of 2.2%.
One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 30.9 km/h with 0.7 s between road users and an adult death risk if hit of 1.6%.
Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

In that video PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 3.7 minutes. Also, 90.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 6 gaps and 0 of them 12 s or more and longest 10.5 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to slow traffic and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch data for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at Quarry Road crossing

We write as the head of the school adjoining the Quarry Road crossing. We commissioned a video review of the crossing covering 20.5 minutes, during which 17 crossings and 16 vehicles were observed.

Of the 17 crossings, 5 of 17 (1 in 3.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 17 (1 in 8.5) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 10.3-56.0% and 1.5-36.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). In total there were 2 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.0 s between a van travelling at 41.7 km/h and a person at the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.1% under Rosén & Sander 2009, and it would be 0.6% if impact were at 20.0 km/h.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.8 s between a car travelling at 18.7 km/h and a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%.

A close pass had a gap of 2.6 s involving a car travelling at 59.8 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.4 s involving a bus travelling at 15.8 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.6 s involving a motorcycle travelling at 28.8 km/h.

Engineering context from the same video is limited. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 20.5 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 68.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are willing to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school. A video-based count was made over 7.9 minutes (474.0 s). In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 40.9 km/h.

The measurements found that 1 of 8 crossings (1 in 8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 0 of 8 within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.3-52.7% and 0.0-36.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-3.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The worst event was a close pass with a time gap of 2.6 s. The vehicle was a van at 40.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts); at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

We note that 59.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 8 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more, the longest 89.0 s. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 7.9, so those rates should be treated with caution.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We would be happy to share the video and the underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

We write about the crossing on River Lane. In 3.6 minutes we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.

6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1-100.0% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 54.1 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.

Worst near-misses recorded were:
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h had 1.1 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 9.8% (Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A serious near-miss with a car at 19.5 km/h had 1.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.6%.
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 14.0 km/h had 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.4%.
A close pass with a car at 39.1 km/h had 1.9 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 1.2%.
A close pass with a car at 16.3 km/h had 1.6 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.3%.

Engineering context is limited. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.6 minutes. Counted was 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.
88.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.9 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the measurement file and discuss the results further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing at the North Avenue crossing used by our school.

A Crossing Watch video recorded 7.6 minutes (456.0 s) at the site and counted 9 pedestrian crossings and 12 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.7 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

In that recording 4 of 9 crossings (1 in 2.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 13.7-78.8% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Of the 4 events within 3 s, 2 were serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

One serious event had a car at 51.1 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.
That speed carries an adult death risk of 9.1% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious event had a van at 27.7 km/h with 1.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
That speed carries an adult death risk of 1.2% if hit, compared with 0.2% at 10.0 km/h.
One close pass had a bus at 57.0 km/h with 2.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
That speed carries an adult death risk of 2.3% if hit.
A second close pass had a car at 19.7 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
That speed carries an adult death risk of 0.2% if hit, compared with 0.2% at 9.5 km/h.
The time gaps are post-encroachment times from SAM tracking and road-plane geometry, and the individual road user was not reviewed.

The video also showed 43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 10 gaps with 4 of them 12 s or more and the longest 82.5 s.
We note the first and last gaps are cut short by the video, and that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video while this recording is 7.6 minutes with 9 crossings and 12 vehicles, so those rates should be treated with caution.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to slow traffic and establish priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school beside Orchard Lane crossing. From video of the crossing we measured 10 crossings and 39 vehicles in 17.2 minutes (1032.0 s), with an 85th percentile speed of 60.5 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.

6 of 10 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 10 (1 in 3.3) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 26.2-87.8% and 6.7-65.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition serious is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. Person first was 4, vehicle first was 2 and both at once was 0.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 53.4 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. Another serious near-miss involved a van at 44.1 km/h with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 14.6 km/h with 0.1 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

One close pass involved a bus at 36.1 km/h with 1.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 31.1 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

For adults hit by a car front, the modelled death risks for those events would be 11.0% for the motorcycle case, 5.1% for the van case, 0.4% for the car case, 1.6% for the bus case and 0.7% for the auto-rickshaw case (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 35 pedestrians and 136 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice, 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 51.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest 38.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to enforce lower speeds at the conflict point and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and measurement log for your review and to discuss further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write on behalf of the school by Quarry Road crossing. Using Crossing Watch video of 10.1 minutes (606.0 s), we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 34 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.9 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing. There were 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The most severe near-miss involved a van at 52.2 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 10.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.
The next involved an auto-rickshaw at 44.9 km/h with 0.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit is 5.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
Another involved a car at 42.9 km/h with 0.6 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit is 4.6%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
Another involved a car at 35.4 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit is 2.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.
The fifth involved a car at 18.6 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit is 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.6 km/h with 0.5% adult death risk.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 10.1 minutes, so we do not use them. In that video 94.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 46.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide pedestrian priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass involved a car at 46.6 km/h with 2.3 s separation, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

I write as head of the school at Mill Street crossing to request safety improvements.

We arranged a video review of the crossing covering 22.6 minutes (1356.0 s). Observation spanned 22.6 minutes with 14 crossings and 21 vehicles tallied. In that time 14 crossings and 21 vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 47.1 km/h. There were 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, with the longest gap at 73.7 s. The count found 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 1 case the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first, with 0 cases of both at once.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.0 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s; the estimated adult death risk if hit is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 15.6 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s. Another close pass involved a motorcycle at 14.1 km/h with a gap of 2.7 s.

Engineering review notes PV² as 0.0 x 10^8, based on 37 pedestrians and 56 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. It also notes that 91.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide a safer crossing for pupils.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the safety of the crossing outside our school at the North Avenue crossing.

In 43.7 minutes of video we recorded 23 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all. 2 of 23 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 23 crossings (1 in 23) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 1.1-28.0% and 0.1-21.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 48.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 7.5% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A second close pass involved a car at 53.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 1.6% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 32 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 9 such gaps and longest 7.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and speed table at this location.

We have the video measurements and are ready to share them to help your assessment. Please let us know how to proceed.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

During 7.7 minutes (462.0 s) of video at Market Street crossing, Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 29 moving vehicles. 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 15.2-72.3% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The recording contained 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 2 times the person was first and 3 times the vehicle was first. Many of the pedestrians were young pupils crossing without adult supervision.

The worst events were: A serious near-miss with PET of 0.8 s involving a car at 32.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had PET of 0.8 s involving a motorcycle at 27.9 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss had PET of 0.6 s involving a motorcycle at 18.0 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at 18.0 km/h. A close pass had PET of 1.9 s involving a bus at 58.6 km/h. For an adult the modelled death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. A further close pass had PET of 2.2 s involving a car at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h. All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front.

Engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this one is 7.7. 48.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap including 1 of 12 s or more and longest 84.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We offer to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

At Orchard Lane crossing, Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded for 11.3 minutes (678.0 s) 7 pedestrian crossings and 7 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.2 km/h.

The video showed 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

1 serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s with a motorcycle at 55.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a car at 40.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6%.

1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car at 33.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0%.

1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.8 s with an auto-rickshaw at 23.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.

1 close pass had a gap of 2.9 s with a car at 12.0 km/h.

In 4 cases the pedestrian arrived first and in 1 case the vehicle arrived first.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 11.3 minutes with 7 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles. 80.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 21.1 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes that 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school at Hill View Road crossing

We commissioned a Crossing Watch survey of the crossing outside the school. Over 24.2 minutes, 10 pedestrian crossings and 14 vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 60.3 km/h. In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian.

The survey found 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The most severe involved a van at 58.7 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s.
The second involved a motorcycle at 53.6 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s.
For an adult hit by a car front, the estimated death risk at those speeds is 16.5% and 11.1% respectively (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 24.2 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour, and 91.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request the raised zebra crossing noted above and are happy to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We measured road use outside our school at Station Road crossing for 37.0 minutes (2220.0 s). In that time we recorded 21 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 49.0 mph.

Of the 21 crossings, 4 of 21 (1 in 5.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 4 of 21 (1 in 5.2) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.4-41.9% and 5.4-41.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 4 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). Of these, 2 were person first and 2 were vehicle first.

The 4 worst serious near-misses were as follows. A bus at 49.3 km/h was 1.0 s apart from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A van at 18.9 km/h was 0.4 s apart from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6%. An auto-rickshaw at 17.2 km/h was 1.4 s apart from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%. A van at 14.2 km/h was 0.2 s apart from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

For context, the engineering review noted PV² = 0.0 x 10^8, based on 34 pedestrians and 13 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. It also noted 41.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 1 gap including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 55.2 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Station Road crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for video analysis at the Garden Road crossing outside our school. In 39.4 minutes (2364.0 s) the camera recorded 18 crossings and 33 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 46.3 km/h. Most vehicles were exceeding the posted speed limit outside the school.

6 of 18 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 18 (1 in 4.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 13.3-59.0% and 6.4-47.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Of these, 4 were serious near-misses under 1.5 s and 2 were close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 2 persons crossed first, 4 vehicles passed first, and 0 were at once.

The worst cases were as follows. A serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a car at 39.4 km/h; modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 3.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with an auto-rickshaw at 35.5 km/h; modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.4%.
A serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with a car at 17.7 km/h; modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.
A serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a car at 16.6 km/h; modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a motorcycle at 13.6 km/h; modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 27 pedestrians and 50 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 39.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 59.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more and longest 89.5 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We have the video and measurement files and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing regarding the safety of the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time were made over 21.9 minutes, equal to 1314.0 s, during which 24 crossings and 39 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. In that period there were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded in 4 cases and vehicle first in 1 case, with 0 cases of both at once.

The worst serious near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious near-miss a bus travelling at 49.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit by the front of a car at that speed the death risk would be 8.0% per Rosen and Sander 2009 for adults 15+ and at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 2nd serious near-miss a car travelling at 28.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.3% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 3rd serious near-miss a bus travelling at 26.0 km/h was 0.2 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.0% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. 2 further close passes had PET of 2.0 s and 2.9 s with vehicle speeds of 12.9 km/h and 33.6 km/h.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 66 pedestrians and 107 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 21.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice with 1.3x inflation in a drone test. 85.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps and 8 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 17.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6 notes that 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone and signs at Lantern Road crossing.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review. Please let us know how you wish to receive them.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.7 s the vehicle was going at 28.6 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.3 s it was going at 56.6 km/h.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
