LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at School Lane crossing

We write regarding pedestrian safety outside our school at School Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video measurements over 37.0 minutes (2220.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 20 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 45.7 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

In that period, 4 of 40 crossings (1 in 10) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, including 2 of 40 (1 in 20) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 2.8-23.7% and 0.6-16.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 65 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in the drone test.

75.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps, 7 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most serious near-miss involved a car at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s to a person, with an adult death risk of 7.1% if hit by a car front at that speed per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A 2nd serious near-miss involved a bus at 23.1 km/h with a gap of 1.4 s to a person, with an adult death risk of 0.8% if hit by a car front at that speed per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A close pass involved a car at 42.4 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s to a person, with an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit by a car front at that speed per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A 2nd close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.5 km/h with a gap of 2.7 s to a person.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review. Please advise on next steps for assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvement requested for the Park Avenue crossing

We write on behalf of the school regarding the pedestrian crossing outside our premises. We commissioned a 10.9 minute video recording (654.0 s) analysed with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In that time there were 7 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles.

The recording showed 5 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 3 of 7 crossings (1 in 2.3) within 1.5 s. 95% exact ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.0-96.3% and 9.9-81.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We classify a gap of less than 1.5 s as a serious near-miss and 1.5-3.0 s as a close pass. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. The vehicle went first in 2 cases and the person went first in 3 cases.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. The van speed was 45.7 km/h. The second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s. The auto-rickshaw speed was 42.2 km/h. The third serious near-miss involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. The car speed was 24.6 km/h.

For close passes, one involved a motorcycle with a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s. The motorcycle speed was 32.4 km/h. The other involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s. The van speed was 16.4 km/h.

For adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), the adult death risk if hit in these events is 5.8% for the van, 4.3% for the auto-rickshaw, 0.9% for the car, 1.4% for the motorcycle, and 0.0% for the second van. At a 20.0 km/h limit the estimated impact speed would be 20.0 km/h for the 3 serious cases with adult death risk of 0.6%, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% risk for the 2 close passes.

The 85th percentile speed was 45.7 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.9 minutes, with counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. 93.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 11 such gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, with the longest 9.7 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We therefore request that the authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at the Park Avenue crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurement file for your review and to discuss the matter further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

I write regarding the Ring Road crossing outside our school. Across 2454.0 s the observation logged 34 crossings while 4 vehicles were seen.

Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 40.9 minutes of video (2454.0 s) showing 34 crossings and 4 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 30.7 km/h. There was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that period 1 vehicle arrived first, 0 pedestrians arrived first and 0 arrived at once.

The worst event was a serious near-miss with a van. The post-encroachment time was 0.7 s. The van was travelling at 25.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 0.9%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%. The road user involved was not reviewed.

For context only, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 50 pedestrians and 6 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 40.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 85.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 1 gap including 1 gap of 12 s or more with the longest gap 70.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to provide a protected crossing and to reduce vehicle speeds.

We would be pleased to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the River Lane crossing. Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 19.2 minutes (1152.0 s) with 15 crossings and 24 vehicles.

During that period 5 of 15 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 15 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-61.6% and 4.3-48.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.5 km/h. Most people crossing there after school are young pupils hurrying home.

The worst serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 49.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 22.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a van at 14.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van at 40.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a car at 47.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.4%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (47 pedestrians and 75 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 19.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 64.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 4 of 12 s or more and the longest 27.1 s (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Lake View Road crossing outside our school. A video survey by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 41.0 minutes (2460.0 s) with 30 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.3 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that recording, 2 of 30 crossings (1 in 15) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 30 (1 in 30) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.8-22.1% and 0.1-17.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s).

The most serious near-miss had a car at 55.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 13.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

The close pass had a car at 53.0 km/h with a gap of 2.6 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, and 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 44 pedestrians and 12 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. Also, 89.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (5 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 63.8 s), noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We have the video and measurements available and would be pleased to share them with your engineering team for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Park Avenue crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 12 pedestrian crossings and 12 moving vehicles in 10.4 minutes and 624.0 s of video.

A second event was a close pass. The gap was 2.4 s. The vehicle was a car travelling at 54.3 km/h.

A third event was a close pass. The gap was 2.1 s. The vehicle was a car travelling at 12.5 km/h.

A fourth event was a close pass. The gap was 2.7 s. The vehicle was a motorcycle travelling at 52.4 km/h.

For context on exposure, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.4. Counted were 12 pedestrian crossings and 12 moving vehicles. 87.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. Most children at this school would be unable to find a safe 12 s gap to cross during busy periods.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for children and staff crossing.

We can share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the School Lane crossing. A video recording of 37.9 minutes (2274.0 s) was analysed with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In that time 6 people crossed and 11 vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 43.5 km/h.

The analysis found 5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person. 4 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9% to 99.6% and 22.3% to 95.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.6 to 11.7 and 1.1 to 10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart, measured as post-encroachment time. There were 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. The person crossed first in 4 cases and the vehicle first in 1 case. Most of the children who use this crossing are under 8 years old and cross without an adult.

The worst events were:
A bus at 36.4 km/h was 0.9 s from the person. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.4% at an impact of 16.1 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 32.7 km/h was 0.5 s from the person. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.9%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 20.9 km/h was 0.6 s from the person. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A motorcycle at 18.7 km/h was 0.2 s from the person. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 18.7 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A bus at 14.0 km/h was 1.8 s from the person. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%, remaining 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 9 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 37.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in drone test). 41.8% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 17.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

We write regarding the Canal Road crossing outside our school. A 1.7 minute video (102.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 60.9 km/h, and found 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 56.3 km/h with 1.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, with an adult death risk of 13.8% if hit by a car front at that speed.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.9 km/h with 0.0 s between, with an adult death risk of 6.4% if hit by a car front.
A third serious near-miss involved a car at 34.7 km/h with 0.2 s between, with an adult death risk of 2.2% if hit by a car front.

For context the engineering note states PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, so this 1.7 minute sample is too short for that calculation. It also notes 86.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 6 such gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more with the longest 48.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the School Lane crossing

We write concerning pedestrian safety outside our school. A video survey of 22.3 minutes (1338.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 20 vehicles. During 22.3 minutes of recording the survey logged 22 crossings and 20 vehicles. 3 of 22 crossings (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 22 (1 in 22) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 0.1-22.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 1 serious near-miss involved a van at 54.3 km/h 1.1 s from the person, with an adult death risk if hit of 11.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). 1 close pass involved a car at 50.9 km/h 1.5 s from the person, with an adult death risk if hit of 9.0%. 1 close pass involved a van at 17.5 km/h 2.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.0%. The 85th percentile speed was 52.9 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (59 pedestrians and 54 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.3 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 64.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (2 gaps, longest 85.8 s; first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school by Cedar Lane crossing and ask you to install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h markings.

A 9.6 minute (576.0 s) video recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. During 576.0 seconds the count logged 16 moving vehicles. In that time 2 of 10 crossings (1 in 5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. The 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 2.5-55.6% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), or 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a car and a person on the same spot 0.6 s apart with the car at 24.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

A second close pass had an auto-rickshaw and a person on the same spot 1.8 s apart with the auto-rickshaw at 21.6 km/h. For an adult the death risk at that speed is 0.3% if hit by a car front, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

Video also shows 92.0% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and longest 10.7 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this recording is 9.6 minutes with 10 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles, so counts are brief.

We request the raised zebra crossing noted above and are happy to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements made by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) at the Park Avenue crossing. In 38.5 minutes of video, equivalent to 2310.0 s, 38 people crossed and 7 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 53.2 km/h.

The video recorded 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded for 4 interactions, vehicle first for 0, and both at once for 0.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 51.2 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 49.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.9%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a bus at 21.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One close pass had a gap of 1.5 s with a car at 52.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.9%.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8, from 59 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also, 64.5% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 27.9 s, noting that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We are willing to share the original video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

There was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). In total 2 events were person-first and 0 were vehicle-first.

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at a 20 km/h limit the impact would be 17.6 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.

The second event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van travelling at 28.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.3%, and at a 20 km/h limit the impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

For context on exposure, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.6. Counted: 4 pedestrian crossings, 3 moving vehicles. Also 63.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 6.9 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. In 2.6 minutes there were 4 crossings and 3 vehicles and the longest gap with no moving vehicle was 6.9 s.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurements on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Mill Street crossing.

We commissioned a video measurement of 7.8 minutes (468.0 s) covering 3 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 20.3 km/h. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to provide a protected crossing and reduce vehicle speeds.

We are willing to share the video and the full measurement report.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the Mill Street crossing. In 44.4 minutes of video we observed 17 crossings and 45 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 44.4 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 14.2-61.7% and 1.5-36.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 32.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.8%. A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 19.7 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 44.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 92.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is 5.2 minutes.

97.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and longest 10.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvement requested for the Park Avenue crossing

We write on behalf of the school regarding the pedestrian crossing outside our premises. We commissioned a 10.9 minute video recording (654.0 s) analysed with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In that time there were seven pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles.

The recording showed 5 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 3 of 7 crossings (1 in 2.3) within 1.5 s. 95% exact ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.0-96.3% and 9.9-81.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We classify a gap of less than 1.5 s as a serious near-miss and 1.5-3.0 s as a close pass. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. The vehicle went first in 2 cases and the person went first in 3 cases.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. The van speed was 45.7 km/h. The second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s. The auto-rickshaw speed was 42.2 km/h. The third serious near-miss involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. The car speed was 24.6 km/h.

For close passes, one involved a motorcycle with a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s. The motorcycle speed was 32.4 km/h. The other involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s. The van speed was 16.4 km/h.

For adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), the adult death risk if hit in these events is 5.8% for the van, 4.3% for the auto-rickshaw, 0.9% for the car, 1.4% for the motorcycle, and 0.0% for the second van. At a 20.0 km/h limit the estimated impact speed would be 20.0 km/h for the 3 serious cases with adult death risk of 0.6%, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% risk for the 2 close passes.

The 85th percentile speed was 45.7 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.9 minutes, with counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. 93.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 11 such gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, with the longest 9.7 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We therefore request that the authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at the Park Avenue crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurement file for your review and to discuss the matter further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Bridge Street crossing

We write as the school beside Bridge Street crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 40.5 minutes of video (2430.0 s) recorded 14 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.8 km/h.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. In 1 case the person was first, in 3 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe was a serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 55.4 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The review defined serious as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. It found 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes. Over 34.7 minutes the count showed 22 crossings and 21 vehicles with 2 serious near-misses and a longest gap of 11.1 s. Person first was 3 and vehicle first was 3.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a van travelling at 54.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 54.5 km/h the death risk is 12.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 29.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 29.4 km/h the death risk is 1.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a van travelling at 56.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 56.1 km/h the death risk is 7.0%.

Engineering review noted PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 38 pedestrians and 36 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 34.7 minutes of video. Its main caveat is that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

The review also noted 51.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and a longest gap of 11.1 s. Its main caveat is that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for school children and staff.

We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We have the video and measurement data and are happy to share them to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Lake View Road crossing outside our school. A video survey by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 41.0 minutes (2460.0 s) with 30 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.3 km/h.

In that recording, 2 of 30 crossings (1 in 15) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 30 (1 in 30) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.8-22.1% and 0.1-17.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s).

The most serious near-miss had a car at 55.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. Most drivers were exceeding the posted speed limit through the crossing. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 13.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

The close pass had a car at 53.0 km/h with a gap of 2.6 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, and 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 44 pedestrians and 12 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. Also, 89.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (5 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 63.8 s), noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We have the video and measurements available and would be pleased to share them with your engineering team for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school I request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone signs outside our gate.

We arranged a video survey of Garden Road crossing for 27.7 minutes (1662.0 s). In that time we recorded 12 crossings by pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 48.4 km/h. Many pupils under 10 cross here alone on their way to school each morning. Of the 12 crossings, 3 of 12 (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 1 of 12 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. Overall there was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s apart).

The most serious near-miss was 0.5 s apart and involved a car at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was 2.2 s apart and involved a car at 46.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.

A third near-miss was 2.0 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 27.4 km/h. At the recorded speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, 85.1% of the recorded time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 77.5 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The scaled estimate is PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 26 pedestrians and 48 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 27.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing and 20 km/h zone to lower speeds and give pedestrians priority. We will share the full video and tracking data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The time gap was 0.4 s.
The vehicle speed was 15.7 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 15.7 km/h the death risk is 0.4% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.
We are willing to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority,

I write on behalf of the school at the Orchard Lane crossing.

A 2.0 minute video recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 22 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 63.3 km/h.

1 close pass involved a car at 36.9 km/h with 1.5 s between the person and the vehicle on the same spot.

A 2nd close pass involved a car at 53.1 km/h with 2.8 s between the person and the vehicle on the same spot.

In engineering terms, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.0 minutes with 7 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles counted. 82.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 36.3 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at the Orchard Lane crossing.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video review of the Park Avenue crossing. In 17.7 minutes of video, 1062.0 s in total, 5 crossings and 6 vehicles were recorded. 4 of 5 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 5 within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 49.8 km/h.

The review found 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

The most serious near-miss had a PET of 0.4 s with an auto-rickshaw at 49.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.3 percent, compared with 0.6 percent at 20.0 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a motorcycle at 29.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.5 percent, compared with 0.3 percent at 10.3 km/h, per the same source.

One close pass had a PET of 2.2 s with a van at 34.3 km/h.

Another close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a motorcycle at 26.7 km/h. A child struck here would face the same 8.3 percent chance of dying.

In that period 90.4 percent of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 22.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The calculated PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 20 vehicles an hour scaled from 17.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table and a 20 km/h zone with signs and markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and the measurements with your engineers and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by the Head of School

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

As Principal of the school by the Lake View Road crossing I write to request safety improvements based on video measurements.

We observed the crossing for 18.8 minutes (1128.0 s) and recorded 5 crossings and 7 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.1 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, with 2 cases where the person went first.

The most serious event was a car passing 0.8 s after a pedestrian at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 0.7% and at an impact of 20.0 km/h it would be 0.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The second event was a car passing 1.8 s after a pedestrian at 39.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 1.6% and at an impact of 0.0 km/h it would be 0.0%.

For context the video scales to PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 16 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour, though a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

About 66.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 9 gaps of which 5 were 12 s or more with a longest gap of 72.5 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. Children at this location face a wait of more than 30 seconds on average before a safe gap appears.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,
We write about the crossing on Mill Street outside our school.
In 21.7 minutes we recorded 30 crossings and 8 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 58.4 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.
3 of 30 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, including 1 within 1.5 s.
The most serious event had a 0.1 s gap with a bus at 53.5 km/h, with modelled 11.1% death risk for an adult hit by a car front.
For an adult hit by a car front at 20.0 km/h impact, the modelled risk is 0.6%.
A separate event had a 2.2 s gap with a car at 39.0 km/h.
Another separate event had a 2.8 s gap with a bus at 19.4 km/h.
Scaled PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 21.7 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.
49.7% of time was in gaps of 6 s or more, noting gaps at start and end are cut short by the video.
We request a raised zebra crossing.
We can share the video and measurements for review.
Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam, I write for our school about safety at the North Avenue crossing. In 39.6 minutes of video, Crossing Watch recorded 7 crossings and 20 vehicles with 85th percentile speed 54.9 km/h. The observation covered 39.6 minutes with 7 crossings and 20 vehicles. By the Crossing Watch definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, with 4 cases where the person entered the spot before the vehicle. A van at 57.5 km/h missed a pedestrian by 0.5 s, with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 15.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009. A car at 28.9 km/h missed a pedestrian by 0.1 s, with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.3% from Rosén & Sander 2009. A car at 52.2 km/h missed a pedestrian by 1.8 s, with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 5.0% from Rosén & Sander 2009. An auto-rickshaw at 56.5 km/h missed a pedestrian by 2.3 s, with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.5% from Rosén & Sander 2009. At a 20.0 km/h limit the 2 serious cases would strike at 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk, and the 2 close-pass cases would strike at 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk. For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 11 pedestrians and 30 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 39.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 96.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 1 gap with longest 49.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. I request a raised zebra crossing at this crossing. I offer to share the video for verification. Yours faithfully, The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing.

A video survey of 43.9 minutes (2634.0 s) recorded 38 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.3 km/h. Nearly 100 children cross here every morning before classes start.

There was 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart respectively.

The most serious near-miss involved a car at 38.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s.

The close pass involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s and speed of 46.0 km/h.

For the serious near-miss, the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 3.2% at 38.9 km/h, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h, based on Rosen & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

In that time there were 0 gaps of 12 s or more and the longest gap was 9.3 s.

We note 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We note PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 52 pedestrians and 15 moving vehicles an hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 43.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We will be pleased to share the video and the full measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by the Principal on dispatch of this letter

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

We measured activity at Garden Road crossing from video of 34.8 minutes, using SAM tracking and post-encroachment time. In that period there were 25 crossings and 13 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.9 km/h. Most drivers were exceeding the posted 30 km/h speed limit during the observation. We recorded 6 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, with 3 where the person was first and 3 where the vehicle was first.

The worst cases were: One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.2 s with a car at 58.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 16.0% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 31.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a bus at 27.2 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.2% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a van at 25.7 km/h and an adult death risk of 1.0% if hit by a car front. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car at 22.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit by a car front. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 43 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 34.8 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. Also, 51.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 gaps and longest gap 8.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone markings and signs at this location. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to record the Garden Road crossing for 3.2 minutes (192.0 s). In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 37.0 km/h.

The definition used was serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes. In 4 cases the person was first to the conflict point, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both arrived at once.

The worst near-miss was a serious conflict with a motorcycle at 38.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 3.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would fall to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was with an auto-rickshaw at 19.3 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Among the close passes, one involved an auto-rickshaw at 14.1 km/h with a gap of 1.5 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4%. Another involved a bus at 16.7 km/h with a gap of 1.6 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4%.

For context, 71.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (6 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 71.0 s). The main caveat is that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 3.2 minutes, and the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians clear priority.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

Crossing Watch tracked 13 crossings and 34 vehicles in 36.4 minutes on River Lane, with 85th speed of 57.9 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

5 of 13 crossings (1 in 2.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 13 (1 in 4.3) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 13.9-68.4% and 5.0-53.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

A car passed within 0.2 s of a person at 54.5 km/h, with 11.9% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A motorcycle passed within 0.1 s of a person at 51.4 km/h, with 9.4% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A bus passed within 0.9 s of a person at 22.6 km/h, with 0.8% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A car passed within 1.7 s of a person at 27.4 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

An auto-rickshaw passed within 1.9 s of a person at 33.8 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 21 pedestrians and 56 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.

46.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 20.6 s, noting video edge truncation.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table on River Lane.

We offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Bridge Street crossing outside our school. The video captured 15 crossings with 17 vehicles over 42.4 minutes.

Measurements were made from 42.4 minutes of video, a duration of 2544.0 s, using Crossing Watch with SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In that period 15 crossings and 17 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 57.2 km/h.

A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The most serious event had a gap of 0.8 s between a van travelling at 53.1 km/h and a pedestrian, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 10.7% from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.

A second event was a close pass with a gap of 1.8 s involving a car travelling at 41.9 km/h, with an adult death risk of 2.0%.

A third event was a close pass with a gap of 2.4 s involving a bus travelling at 49.4 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

A fourth event was a close pass with a gap of 2.1 s involving a motorcycle travelling at 25.6 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 21 pedestrians and 24 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 42.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

43.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 72.0 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a safe place to cross.

We have the video and tracking data available and are happy to share it with you for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing as the school using Market Street crossing. We commissioned video monitoring of the crossing.

Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 16.6 minutes (996.0 s). In that time 26 crossings and 41 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 53.2 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the near-misses, 3 were person-first, 2 were vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 54.0 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 11.5% per Rosen & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 43.9 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 5.0% per the same source.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 28.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% per the same source.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 26.6 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.1% per the same source.
One close pass involved a van at 36.8 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% per the same source.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 148 vehicles an hour scaled from 16.6 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. Also, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 7 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.6 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We arranged a video survey of Garden Road crossing for 27.7 minutes (1662.0 s). In that time we recorded 12 crossings by pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 48.4 km/h. Of the 12 crossings, 3 of 12 (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 1 of 12 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. Overall there was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s apart).

The most serious near-miss was 0.5 s apart and involved a car at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was 2.2 s apart and involved a car at 46.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.

A third near-miss was 2.0 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 27.4 km/h. At the recorded speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, 85.1% of the recorded time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 77.5 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The scaled estimate is PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 26 pedestrians and 48 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 27.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing and 20 km/h zone to lower speeds and give pedestrians priority. We will share the full video and tracking data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing regarding the safety of the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time were made over 21.9 minutes, equal to 1314.0 s, during which 24 crossings and 39 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision. In that period there were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Person first was recorded in 4 cases and vehicle first in 1 case, with 0 cases of both at once.

The worst serious near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious near-miss a bus travelling at 49.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit by the front of a car at that speed the death risk would be 8.0% per Rosen and Sander 2009 for adults 15+ and at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 2nd serious near-miss a car travelling at 28.6 km/h was 0.1 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.3% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. In a 3rd serious near-miss a bus travelling at 26.0 km/h was 0.2 s apart from a pedestrian; if an adult were hit at that speed the death risk would be 1.0% and at 20.0 km/h the risk would be 0.6%. 2 further close passes had PET of 2.0 s and 2.9 s with vehicle speeds of 12.9 km/h and 33.6 km/h.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 66 pedestrians and 107 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 21.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice with 1.3x inflation in a drone test. 85.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps and 8 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 17.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6 notes that 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone and signs at Lantern Road crossing.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review. Please let us know how you wish to receive them.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal
Approved by The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Hill View Road crossing

We write regarding pedestrian safety outside our school at Hill View Road crossing.

Crossing Watch recorded 19 crossings and 12 vehicles in 44.5 minutes. 2 of 19 crossings (1 in 9.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 19 (1 in 9.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.3-33.1% and 1.3-33.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. The 85th percentile speed was 46.5 km/h.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 43.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The other serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 41.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.0% per the same source.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 26 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice by 1.3x in our drone test. 45.6% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 such gaps and 1 of 12 s or more, longest 88.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide pedestrian priority.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

I am writing on behalf of our school about safety at the Canal Road crossing. A 6.4 minute video recording, duration 384.0 s, at the crossing measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 44 moving vehicles.

85th percentile speed was 60.5 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.5 s the vehicle was going at 51.9 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.1 s it was going at 54.4 km/h. Analysis used SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

In that period, 6 of 6 crossings, 1 in 1, had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s. 5 of 6, 1 in 1.2, were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1 to 100.0% and 35.9 to 99.6% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 2.2 to 13.1 and 1.6 to 11.7 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

2 crossings had the person first and 4 had the vehicle first, with 0 both at once. 1 was a close pass and 5 were serious near-misses.

Details of the serious near-misses, with adult death risk if hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus, car fronts:

The first involved a bus at 54.4 km/h with a time gap of 0.5 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 11.8%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The second involved a van at 51.9 km/h with a time gap of 0.1 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 9.7%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The third involved a van at 31.6 km/h with a time gap of 1.0 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 1.7%, compared to impact at 17.9 km/h and 0.5% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The fourth involved a motorcycle at 26.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 1.1%, compared to impact at 6.3 km/h and 0.2% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

The fifth involved a motorcycle at 20.5 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 0.6%, compared to impact at 20.0 km/h and 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.4, with 6 crossings and 44 vehicles counted. 60.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 17.6 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch data for your review. Thank you for your consideration.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal per school authorization process

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the School Lane crossing.

In 34.0 minutes of video (2040.0 s) we recorded 3 crossings and 4 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 28.6 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%. The road user involved was not reviewed.

UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

We write about Orchard Lane crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch measured the crossing for 3.4 minutes (204.0 s) using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.
Counted in that time were 7 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 59.7 km/h. A child hit at that speed would have a 12% chance of being killed.
PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 3.4 minutes.
96.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 52.4 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.
UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 4 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s) were recorded.
A serious near-miss involved a car at 38.9 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.
A second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 21.4 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
A close pass involved a bus at 53.7 km/h with 2.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
Another close pass involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 2.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
A further close pass involved a car at 31.5 km/h with 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.
We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch review of 30.3 minutes (1818.0 s) of video at North Avenue crossing recorded 17 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 40.8 km/h. In that period 2 of 17 crossings (1 in 8.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, of which 1 of 17 (1 in 17) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.5-36.4% and 0.1-28.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s between the person and a bus travelling at 36.8 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates that an adult hit by a car front at that speed has a 2.7% death risk, compared with 0.2% death risk at an impact of 7.5 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A second close pass had a gap of 2.9 s from a bus travelling at 28.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 30.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. In the recording, 47.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 8 gaps including 6 of 12 s or more with longest 13.6 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We hold the video and tracking data and would be pleased to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Park Avenue crossing.

In 25.2 minutes of video we recorded 40 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 27.8 km/h. There were 4 gaps of 6 s or more, 4 of those were 12 s or more, with the longest gap at 68.5 s.

There was 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s respectively. In 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

If the vehicle had been limited to 20.0 km/h the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.
The second event was a close pass involving a car at 22.9 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.0%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 95 pedestrians and 19 moving vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 25.2 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour. IRC:103-2012 cl. 6.7.4.1.2 notes a controlled crossing may be warranted above 1 x 10^8 on an undivided road, 2 x 10^8 on a divided road.
43.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school at Ring Road crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Ring Road crossing.

Our 26.1 minutes of video (1566.0 s) recorded 23 crossings and 22 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.3 km/h. Of the 23 crossings, 3 of 23 (1 in 7.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 23 (1 in 7.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.8-33.6% and 2.8-33.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). All 3 events were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The most severe had a PET of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 51.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.1%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 33.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a van at 14.2 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, which at 20 km/h limit corresponds to an impact of 14.2 km/h and 0.4% risk.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 53 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 90.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 24.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video and UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and provide protected crossing time. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The car was travelling at 21.6 km/h. For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 gives a death risk of 0.7% at that speed, and 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h at a 20.0 km/h limit. The 85th percentile speed in the video was 25.0 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Hill View Road crossing.

A video of 7.7 minutes (462.0 s) recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 14.7 km/h. In that recording 2 of 4 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 4 (1 in 4) was within 1.5 s.

1 crossing was a serious near-miss with a gap of 1.0 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw travelling at 14.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that case would be 14.3 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%. 

1 crossing was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s with a car travelling at 15.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that case would be 13.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.3%.

Engineering review is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 7.7 minutes, with 4 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles counted. In the recording 65.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, measured as 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 3 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 36.1 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow traffic and protect children crossing. Local parents report that children regularly have to run to avoid traffic at this crossing. We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) over 7.0 minutes (420.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.9 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 4 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s).

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 19.1 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with a car at 18.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a bus at 56.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 1.0% if hit by a car front.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s with a car at 16.9 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s with a car at 36.3 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.0. Counted: 8 pedestrian crossings, 23 moving vehicles. Also, 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 3 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 73.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that the authority install the raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review. Across 7.0 minutes, 4 crossings saw the person move first while 2 saw the vehicle move first.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the River Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the River Lane crossing outside our school. Measurements from 20.0 minutes of video by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 27 pedestrian crossings and 7 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.2 km/h.

There was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. The worst case had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. It involved a bus. Many of our young pupils must sprint across to dodge fast traffic. The vehicle speed in that event was 54.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 81 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.0 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in the drone test. Also, 91.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and underlying measurements on request.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

As Principal of the school by the Lake View Road crossing I write to request safety improvements based on video measurements.

We observed the crossing for 18.8 minutes (1128.0 s) and recorded five crossings and 7 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.1 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss and 1 close pass, with 2 cases where the person went first.

The most serious event was a car passing 0.8 s after a pedestrian at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 0.7% and at an impact of 20.0 km/h it would be 0.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The second event was a car passing 1.8 s after a pedestrian at 39.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed would be 1.6% and at an impact of 0.0 km/h it would be 0.0%.

For context the video scales to PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 16 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour, though a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

About 66.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 9 gaps of which 5 were 12 s or more with a longest gap of 72.5 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
